GENERAL INFORMATION

http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION

may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24

Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting,
please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting.
Council Chambers are wheelchair accessible.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  This Ordinance was reviewed pursuant to CEQA. Adopting this Ordinance is exempt from further

  facilities; minor temporary use of land; minor alterations in land use; new construction of small

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Shawn Igoe, Director of Public Works
 SUBJECT:  Receive and File Staff Report Summarizing the Status of Emergency
  Repairs of the Monterey Pass Road Water Line

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receive and File the staff report summarizing the status of emergency repairs of
  the Monterey Pass Road water line; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

BACKGROUND:
On August 17, 2022, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2022-R69 authorizing the City
Manager to take necessary measures for emergency repair of a water main line on
Monterey Pass Road. Recurring water main leaks in several areas within Monterey Pass
Road between the intersections of Vagabond Drive and Brightwood street resulted in
extensive infrastructure damage to the roadway and necessary water main pipe repairs
to ensure continued water service to residences and businesses in the area.

On August 29, 2022, the City contracted with Cannon Corporation for professional
engineering services to prepare design plans and specifications for the water pipeline
replacement. Cannon provided the City with complete plans to replace the existing 12-
inch water transmission line in December which was identified in the December 21, 2022
staff report update for this project.

Following the adoption of the emergency resolution, staff contacted potential contractors
and identified Ferreira Coastal Construction (Ferreira) in September 2022 as a qualified
contractor that also had the resources and availability for the construction phase of this
project. Ferreira worked closely with the City and Cannon Corporation during the design
phase to provide input on design, constructability, and material availability.

The design phase began with a field survey, potholing and research of underground
infrastructure that affect the placement of the proposed piping system which took several
months due to the existing infrastructure overlaps. Various design alternatives were
studied to address conflicting utilities with the Southern California Edison substation
underground electrical, storm drain lines and sewer mains which impacted the placement
of the new water main. Additional research of available material and cost was conducted

during the months of December and January to ensure the project could be expedited
due to the significant material delivery delays.

Design work of this type of project typically takes at least six months to complete. Final
design, however, was completed in under four months along with a final material list being
developed, researched and evaluated, leading to an approximate reduction in four to six
months of time for this project to be completed. By adopting the emergency resolution
and reducing the typical timeline, impacts to essential services and damages to public
and private property are being mitigated. The City received pricing and lead times for
material from three vendors and worked with Ferreira to evaluate the City’s best option
based on cost, lead time and availability of parts and material. Staff ordered the material
required for the project in January and February 2023. Construction has now started and
is scheduled to be complete by October 2023.

Typical emergency projects can be completed within a short period of time; this project is
significantly different as there is approximately one-mile of 12-inch water main that failed
in several locations and continues to see failure points. These failures led to businesses
that operate around the clock to be left without essential public services during these
repairs in addition to limited access to their businesses. These failures have led to
significant damages to the roadway which require additional work and material to restore.
There were additional delays that impacted this project related to receiving material with
the continued supply chain challenges that continue to impact projects such as this one.
Additionally, the recent rain has impacted construction citywide.

As part of the City’s outreach efforts, the construction manager visited business along the
project area prior to the start of the project to notify them of the upcoming construction.
The Economic Development Division also mailed out letters to businesses that may be
impacted by this project. Message boards were placed within the project area before
construction to alert drivers of the impact to their commutes. The City will continue to
provide project updates to the community for the duration of the project through the City
website, social media, and City Council meetings. A dedicated webpage was created on
the city’s website as, www.Montereypark.ca.gov/Montereypass, to inform the public about
the project and provide progress updates. Residents and businesses can also sign up to
receive project updates by subscribing to NIXLE, by texting "MPSS" to 888777.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Maychelle Yee, City Clerk
 SUBJECT:  Professional Municipal Clerks Week Resolution

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting a Resolution declaring the week of April 30 – May 6, 2023 as Professional
  Municipal Clerks Week in Monterey Park; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Office of the City Clerk is celebrating the week of April 30 – May 6, 2023 as
Professional Municipal Clerks Week. This week, sponsored by the International Institute
of Municipal Clerk’s (IIMC) and celebrated annually, honors and recognizes the Municipal
Clerk profession as a vital part of local government celebrated throughout the world
including the United States, Canada and 15 other countries. We are enlisting your
support in the form of a resolution to honor Professional Municipal Clerks for providing
supports to the Council, departmental staff, other agencies, and residents of Monterey
Park.

BACKGROUND:
Historically, the Office of the City Clerk recognizes and celebrates the hard work,
commitment and devotion Professional Municipal Clerks provide to ensure the integrity
and democracy process of Monterey Park residents.

None.

   RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  MONTEREY PARK DECLARING APRIL 30 THROUGH
  MAY 6, 2023, PROFESSIONAL MUNICIPAL CLERKS
  WEEK IN MONTEREY PARK

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A.  The Monterey Park Office of the City Clerk is celebrating the week of
  April 30 through May 6, 2023 as Professional Municipal Clerks Week.
  This week, sponsored by the International Institute of Municipal
  Clerks (IIMC), honors and recognizes the Municipal Clerk profession
  as a vital part of local government celebrated throughout the world
  including the United States, Canada and 15 other countries.

  B.  In 1984 and in 1994, Presidents Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton,
  respectively, signed a Proclamation officially declaring Professional
  Municipal Clerks Week the first full week of May and recognizing the
  essential role Professional Municipal Clerks play in local
  government.

  C.  Although it is one of the oldest positions in local government, few
  people realize the vital services Professional Municipal Clerks
  perform for their community. Primarily, they act as the cornerstone
  of their council. They also prepare the council agendas, record and
  index minutes and maintain the ordinances and resolutions files.
  Other responsibilities include keeping the official records of the city
  and conducting local elections.

  D.  The Office of the City Clerk provides the professional link between
  the residents, the local governing bodies and agencies of
  government at other levels. Professional Municipal Clerks serve as
  the information center on functions of local government and
  community acting as the contact office for general information, public
  records requests, receipt of claims and subpoenas.

  E.  Professional Municipal Clerks have pledged to be ever mindful of
  their neutrality and impartiality, rendering equal service to all and
  continually strive to improve the administration of the affairs of the
  Office of the City Clerk.

  F.  We are confident that you will stand behind the commitment and
  devotion Professional Municipal Clerks provide to ensure the
  integrity and democracy process of Monterey Park residents.

  G.  The City of Monterey Park recognizes and celebrates the hard work
  of these dedicated professionals and declare April 30 through May
  6, 2023 as Professional Municipal Clerk Week in Monterey Park,
  honoring and recognizing the essential role Professional Municipal
  Clerks play in local government.

SECTION 2: Electronic Signatures. This Resolution may be executed with electronic
signatures in accordance with Government Code §16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

SECTION 3: Recordation. The Mayor, or presiding officer, is authorized to sign this
Resolution signifying its adoption by the City Council of the City of Monterey Park and the
City Clerk, or her duly appointed deputy, may attest thereto.

SECTION 4: Effective Date. This Resolution will become effective immediately upon
adoption and will remain effective unless repealed or superseded.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Every April, The Office for Victims of Crime leads communities throughout the country in
their annual observances of National Crime Victims’ Rights Week. This year National
Crime Victims’ Rights week is observed between April 23rd – April 29th. We are enlisting
your support in the form of a resolution to honor all victims of crime but especially those
victims of the January 21, 2023 shooting incident.

BACKGROUND:

In 1981, the President’s Task Force on Victims of Crime was established to help those
who had experienced crime and their families. This was an important step toward the
protection of and support for victims’ rights. Over the years, crime victims’ rights have
evolved. Dedicated professionals have worked to develop support and services for
survivors that are more holistic, trauma-informed, and effective at overcoming systemic
barriers that certain communities face in prosecuting offenders and obtaining justice.
During National Crime Victims’ Rights week, our nation renews our commitment to
providing survivors of crime the support they need to heal.

RECOMMENDATION:

  1. Receiving and filing this report;

  Monterey Park and authorizing the City Manager to take all practical actions
  needed to implement the efficient recruitment and retention of persons for
  employment; and

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City continues to utilize the employment emergency to expedite recruitment
processes to fill vacancy positions. Since February 2023, the City has filled a Facility
Maintenance Supervisor, Water Utility Maintenance Worker, Maintenance Worker,
promoted Police Captain, two Lieutenants, Sergeant, four Corporals, Senior
Maintenance Worker, Crew Leader, and Senior Librarian.

Since December 2022, 11 full-time and 14 part-time employees have resigned or
retired. The recruitment trend continues to be an employee’s job market with various
options for candidates to consider when looking for employment. The data from the
U.S. labor market shows a large gap between job openings and workforce participation
in 2022, translating into challenges for employers to attract quality candidates and retain
current employees. In October 2022, the City was recruiting for 46 full-time positions,
December 2022 – 39 positions, February 2023 – 37 positions and the City continues to
recruit for 29 vacant full-time positions. Staff recommends extending the employment
emergency order due to the recruitment challenges for critical vacancies in the Public
Works Department and other departments.

During the months of the employment emergency the City recruited or retained
employees in different ways:

  A.  Since the City Council officially terminated the COVID-19 local emergency

  Maintenance Worker; Director of Public Works; Facilities Maintenance

  the smooth operation of municipal services including, for example, providing
  potable drinking water, and ensuring public safety;

  information (see, e.g., “Quantifying the Nation’s Workforce Crisis – State of
  American Business 2022 Update” [January 10, 2022] published by the United
  States Chamber of Commerce [www.uschamber.com/workforce/quantifying-the-

  recruiting qualified employees is nationwide;

  testing; interviewing; and background check;

RECOMMENDATION:

  1. Adopting a resolution authorizing the City Manager, or designee, to apply for,
  receive, and appropriate grant funds for the California State Library Building
  Forward Library Facilities Improvement Grant
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The California State Library Building Forward Library Facilities Improvement Grant
provides competitive grants of up to $10 million to local libraries to support capital projects
addressing critical maintenance needs, improving energy efficiency and sustainability,
and expanding access digitally and physically.

lf adopted, the proposed resolution would authorize the City Manager, or designee, to
apply for the Building Forward Grant, to execute the grant agreement, and to implement
a budget amendment if the City is awarded funds. The deadline to apply is May 18, 2023,
funds will be awarded in the fall of 2023 and the project completion date is June 30, 2027.

BACKGROUND:
The California State Library Building Forward Library Facilities Improvement Program is
the largest single investment made by the state in California’s public libraries. There is
$179 million available for this round of grants, which is significantly less than the expected
amount of requested funding. Accordingly, the State Library anticipates that they may
reduce the amount requested by successful applicants. Additionally, project requests
submitted for libraries located in high-poverty areas of the state will be prioritized for
funding. Currently high need maintenance projects within the Library are being identified
by City staff. Although libraries may apply for up to $10 million in grant funding, staff
anticipates that our total request will be in the $2-3 million-dollar range.

Dear Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council,

It gives me great pleasure to strongly recommend Victoria Chavez-Calderon for a Memorial Tree in the City of
Monterey Park, California. I have known her for more than 30 years and over the course of that time I have seen
her defend our immigrant communities, fight for diversity, and uplift all Monterey Park residents.

More than three decades ago, the City of Monterey Park was facing an ugly anti-immigrant English only
movement that was tearing our community apart. At the time, a vocal group of long-established residents
resented the new immigrants moving into town and demanded English only signs across the community, books
in the library, and passed a resolution declaring that only English should be spoken in the city. This was a dark
time for our city, but it was leaders like Victoria that bravely stood up and pushed back. She was one of the
strongest critics against this movement and fiercely defended our immigrant communities. Together we worked
alongside a multiethnic coalition who successfully fought to overturn the resolution and set us on a new path.

In the following years Victoria continued her advocacy for diversity by establishing the Morelia, Mexico sister
cities commission. In doing so, she brought pride to many Mexican American residents and helped promote
greater cultural understanding between two different nations and within our own neighborhoods.

At the same time, Victoria has consistently worked hard to build a stronger Monterey Park community. As a
member of the Community Participation Commission, she has created opportunities for residents to come
together and enjoy cultural performances, historic exhibits, and many other local events. In her capacity she has
also led trips to the Hollywood Bowl, visited seniors at the Langley Senior Center, and engaged our youth so
that they can also participate in community activities.

Victoria Chavez-Calderon has spent her entire life defending immigrant communities, advocating for diversity,
and building a stronger Monterey Park. She is more than deserving of a Memorial Tree in her name and I am
proud to strongly recommend her for this honor.

Sincerely,

JUDY CHU, Ph.D.

   I. INTRODUCTION

  This Monterey Park Market Place Specific Plan (Specific Plan) was prepared in conformity with
  Government Code § 65451, et seq. Together with zoning regulations adopted by the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (MPMC) and other Applicable Law (defined below), this Specific Plan sets
  forth the regulations for the development and operation of the Monterey Park Market Place
  project (Project or the Market Place).

  Pursuant to Government Code § 65450, a specific plan must include text and a diagram or
  diagrams, which specify all of the following in detail:

  •  The distribution, location, and extent of the uses of land, including open space within the
  area covered by the plan.
  •  The proposed distribution, location, extent, and intensity of major components of public
  and private transportation, sewage, water, drainage, solid waste disposal, energy and
  other essential facilities proposed to be located within the land area covered by the plan
  and needed to support the land uses described in the plan.
  •  Standards and criteria by which development will proceed, and standards for the
  conservation, development, and utilization of natural resources, where applicable.
  •  A program of implementation measures, including regulations, programs, public works
  projects and financing measures necessary to carry out the above items.
  •  A discussion of the relationship of the Specific Plan to the General Plan.

  This Specific Plan is compatible and consistent with the goals and policies outlined in the City of
  Monterey Park’s General Plan (General Plan). This Specific Plan will further the goals and policies
  of the General Plan as more fully described below.

  This Specific Plan was prepared to provide the essential relationship between the policies of the
  General Plan and actual development in the Project area. By functioning as a regulatory
  document, the Specific Plan provides a means of implementing the General Plan. All future
  development within the Specific Plan boundaries must be consistent with the standards set forth
  in this document.

A.  SPECIFIC PLAN AREA
  This Specific Plan regulates real property (a triangular-shaped parcel consisting of approximately
  63.68 acres) located in the southeast portion of the City of Monterey Park, in the County of Los
  Angeles, State of California, immediately north of the Pomona Freeway, State Route 60 (Pomona
  Freeway), and west of Paramount Boulevard as shown on Figure 1 (Specific Plan Area).

  and Monterey Park Retail Partners, LLC to allow the development of the Monterey Park Market
  Place. The Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan covered the same geographical location as

   II. SPECIFIC PLAN OVERVIEW

A.  PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY OF THE SPECIFIC PLAN
  This Specific Plan is intended to provide for the orderly and efficient development of the Specific
  Plan Area in accordance with the provisions of the General Plan. In conjunction with the General
  Plan, the Specific Plan implements the plan for the physical development of the Specific Plan Area
  and a guide to all future development within the plan area.

  A Specific Plan may be prepared for any defined geographic area, which might benefit from
  specialized land use regulations and development standards.

  The Specific Plan provides for development within the Specific Plan Area and establishes the
  permitted uses, development intensity, site planning and development standards, design and
  architecture, landscaping, signs, refuse facilities, access and circulation, parking, and trip
  reduction measures of the Project.

B.  SPECIFIC PLAN SCOPE AND GOALS
  Implementation of General Plan goals and policies will occur through the establishment of land
  use designations, traffic circulation patterns, development policies, and the identification of
  backbone infrastructure necessary to support the planned intensity of development.

  To achieve this purpose, the Specific Plan has the following goals:

  1. Establish the planning concept, design theme, development regulations, and procedures
  necessary to achieve an orderly and compatible development;
  2. Implement the goals, policies, and objectives of the General Plan;
  3. Establish a framework to create a successful Project with a mix of predominantly retail
  uses with retail-supporting uses, such as Last Mile Distribution Center and Warehouse
  uses;
  4. Meet changing market demands for more home delivery by allowing car sales, Last Mile
  Distribution Center and Warehouse uses;
  5. Facilitate the full build-out of the Specific Plan Area; and
  6. Provide clear design guidelines and standards to allow for flexibility in the implementation
  and build-out of planned development within the Specific Plan area.

  III. OVERVIEW OF LAND USE PLAN

A.  DEVELOPMENT CONCEPT
  The Specific Plan provides a framework for developing approximately 63.68-acres in the
  southeast portion of Monterey Park and an additional nine-acre area of easements owned by
  SCE. The development is a highway oriented commercial project consisting of approximately
  600,000 square feet of commercial uses and/or distribution and warehouse uses, with adequate
  supporting parking spaces and associated landscaping, inclusive of existing and proposed

  11

  Page 89 of 245
   development within the Specific Plan Area. Collectively, the Specific Plan Area and SCE easement
  areas are referred to as the “Site.”

  Development may be based on four Conceptual Development Plans, set forth in Section V.D.2,
  below, or as otherwise allowed under the Specific Plan.

  Build-out of the Specific Plan would provide a range of economic, fiscal, and quality of life benefits
  to the City.

B.  LAND USE PLAN
  This Specific Plan provides a framework of infrastructure and urban design that will
  accommodate the wide range of commercial/industrial uses anticipated over the life of the
  Project while remaining consistent with Monterey Park’s suburban character.

  New development of Individual Projects may be based on one of the Conceptual Development
  Plans (see Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, and 4D). Development options other than the Conceptual
  Development Plans are permissible as set forth in the Specific Plan.

C.  GRADING CONCEPT
  Grading plans for an Individual Project’s building pads, roadways, pedestrian paths, water, sewer,
  and other utilities will be developed as needed for each Individual Project. Grading may consist
  of over excavation of soils beneath proposed buildings, to a depth of three to four feet, to remove
  unsuitable building material.

  Limited import for Individual Projects may be necessary, and is permissible, to stabilize soils
  depending upon the final geotechnical recommendations of a soils engineer.

  All grading must be accomplished pursuant to a Grading Plan that contains the following:

  a. Best management practices (BMPs).
  b. Non-paved areas must be revegetated or restored promptly after installation of utilities
  using drought-resistant, fast-growing vegetation that would quickly stabilize exposed
  ground surfaces. Alternative materials rather than reseeding (e.g., gravel) may be used in
  accordance with the Director’s direction.
  c. Runoff must be conveyed in accordance with the approved site drainage plans.
  d. Energy dissipaters or similar devices may be required at the end of drainpipe outlets to
  minimize erosion during storm events.
  e. Grading cannot occur during the wet season (November 1-April 15) unless erosion control
  devices acceptable to the City are implemented.

  12

   f. Grading must be completed such that permanent drainage away from foundations and
  slabs is provided and so that water does not pond near proposed structures or
  pavements.

  IV. EXISTING UTILITIES AND INFRASTRUCTURE

  The intent of this Section is to ensure that the Specific Plan Area is developed to support
  development of the proposed land uses and that on-site and off-site infrastructure systems have
  adequate capacity to serve the Project at build-out.

  Development of Individual Projects may require improving existing infrastructure and services in
  the Specific Plan Area. Basic utilities, including, water, sewer, and other utilities already exist on-
  site.

  The Government Code requires that a specific plan include text and diagrams that specify “the
  proposed distribution, location, and extent and intensity of major components of public and
  private transportation, sewage, water, drainage, solid waste disposal, energy, and other essential
  facilities proposed to be located within the area covered by the plan and needed to support the
  land uses described in the plan.”

  This Section of the Specific Plan fulfills this requirement and meets the MPMC requirements for
  the preparation of specific plans. In addition, this Section facilitates orderly development by
  identifying “backbone” utility infrastructure needed to support the proposed development.

  Site Planning Standards are those provisions that affect the site planning of an Individual
  Project. The categories that relate to this Specific Plan are building height, setback, and
  parking.

  1. Building Height – Building height within the Specific Plan Area is limited to 80 feet, as
  measured from the adjacent grade. Architectural features are allowed to project an
  additional 15 feet above the roof line.
  2. Floor Area Ratio – Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is limited to 0.65.
  3. Setback – The Site is surrounded by SCE’s right-of-way and the Pomona Freeway. The Site
  must maintain a 30-foot setback from property lines adjacent to a public Right-of-Way
  and the Freeway. The Specific Plan Area is allowed to have zero-foot setback from
  property lines adjacent to the SCE Easement Areas. All setbacks must be clear to the sky
  but may include roadways, utility infrastructure, loading, parking, landscaping, and fences
  and walls.
  4. Aisle Width – Parking areas must use a minimum of 24-foot aisle widths for two-way
  configurations and a minimum of 12-foot widths for one-way configurations. Parking area
  aisle widths must be a minimum provide for a minimum 25-foot back-out area for parking
  spaces. Standard parking stalls must be a minimum 9’ x 18’ stall size. Compact parking
  spaces are permitted pursuant to Section V.E.5 below.
  5. Parking Standards – The Site must comply with Applicable Law for handicapped parking
  area. All such parking stalls must be located reasonably near the storefronts for easy
  access and be striped and signed in a manner clearly showing the layouts of each parking
  space.
  6. Compact Spaces – The Site may include compact parking spaces. Compact spaces are
  those reduced from the standard 9’ x 18’ to 7 ‘ 6 “ x 16’. Compact stalls may not total
  more than 22% of the total required parking space on the site and must be clearly marked
  as “COMPACT,” with a site layout design approved by the Director.
  7. Loading Standards – Every warehousing/storage/light industrial tenant space must be
  provided with at least one off-street loading dock, bay, or space for every 25,000 square
  feet of gross floor area. The loading space must be a minimum of 12’ width x 40’ length x
  14’ height. Loading docks or bays must be provided for users that require truck loading
  spaces and that contain more than 50,000 square feet of floor area. Truck loading bays or
  docks must be located to allow for trucks to back into bays. All loading bays must be
  screened from sight from the public right-of-way.

I.  REFUSE FACILITIES
  For proper waste management practices, trash enclosures and/or equipment will be strategically
  located in the rear of each building, if feasible. Gates must be six-foot-high. Major tenants may
  have their own waste management areas within their building footprints to maintain the proper
  visual aesthetics of the Specific Plan Area. Public waste management will be accomplished by
  placing on-site furniture, such as waste receptacles and ash urns, throughout the Site. To
  minimize solid waste generated by the Project, the following measures must be implemented:

  1. Construction Phase – During Project construction, the following practices must be
  implemented to the maximum extent feasible:
  a. Off-site locations for construction waste exported from the Site and options for
  disposal of excess material should be identified. These options may include recycling
  of materials on-Site, sale to a broker or contractor, sale to a project in the vicinity, or
  transport to an environmentally cleared landfill.

  28

  Page 106 of 245
   b. Individual Project applicants should offer recyclable building materials, such as
  asphalt or concrete for sale or removal by private firms or public agencies for use in
  construction of other projects, if all cannot be reused on the Site.
  2. Operation Phase – During Project operations, the following practices must be
  implemented, to the maximum extent feasible, by the Project tenants within their
  buildings and will be specified in lease agreements between the Applicant and individual
  tenants:
  a. Recovery of materials such as aluminum and cardboard;
  b. Collection of office paper for recycling;
  c. Collection of polystyrene (foam) cups for recycling;
  d. Collection of glass, plastics, kitchen grease, laser printer toner cartridges, oil,
  batteries, and scrap metal for recycling or recovery.
  3. Design Features – The Applicant(s), tenants, and/or owner(s) of the Specific Plan Area are
  required to implement design features to support solid waste reduction programs, such
  as:
  a. Identifying the location and design of on-site recycling facilities;
  b. Providing on-site recycling receptacles to encourage recycling;
  c. Facilitating cardboard recycling (especially in retail areas) by providing adequate
  space and centralized locations for collection and bailing;
  d. Providing trash compactors for non-recycling materials to reduce the total volume of
  solid waste and the number of trips required for collection; and
  e. Providing on-site recycling receptacles in feasible locations accessible to the public to
  encourage recycling for all businesses, employees, and patrons.

K.  TRIP REDUCTION AND TRAVEL DEMAND MEASURES
  Reduction of trip and travel demand measures are provided in accordance with Applicable Law.
  Before any development is approved within the Specific Plan Area, Applicant(s) must provide for
  all of the following applicable transportation demand management and trip reduction measures
  to promote better air quality. The Project must comply with the Development Standards for

  29

  Page 107 of 245
 Nonresidential Development of 100,000 square feet and also provide all of the following
measures to the satisfaction of the Director and Public Works Director:

  1. Displayed Information – A bulletin board, display case, or kiosk displaying transportation
  information located where the greatest number of employees are likely to see it.
  Information must include, without limitation, the following:
  a. Current maps, routes and schedules for public transit serving the Site;
  b. Telephone numbers for referrals on transportation information, including numbers
  for regional ridesharing agency and local transit operators;
  c. Ridesharing promotional materials supplied by commuter-oriented organizations;
  d. Bicycle route and facility information, including regional/local bicycle maps and
  bicycle information;
  e. A list of facilities available for car-poolers, vanpoolers, bicyclists, transit riders and
  pedestrians at the Site.
  2. Van Pool – Not less than 10% of employee parking area must be located as close as is
  practical to the employee entrance(s), and be reserved for use by potential
  carpool/vanpool vehicles, without displacing handicapped and customer parking needs.
  A statement that preferential carpool/vanpool spaces for employees are available and a
  description of the method for obtaining such spaces must be included on the required
  transportation information board. Spaces will be signed/striped as demand warrants.
  Adequate turning radii and parking space dimensions shall also be included in van pool
  parking areas.
  3. Bicycles – Bicycle racks or other secure bicycle parking must be provided:
  a. To accommodate four bicycles per the first fifty thousand square feet of
  nonresidential developments;
  b. One bicycle per each additional fifty thousand square feet of nonresidential
  development. Calculations, which result in a fraction of 0.5 or higher, shall be rounded
  up to the nearest whole number;
  c. Bicycle facilities, such as showers, lockers, and changing spaces, must be provided for
  every tenant employing more than 80 employees per shift, and separate facilities for
  all genders must be provided for tenants employing more than 160 employees per
  shift;
  d. A bicycle parking facility may also be fully enclosed space or locker accessible only to
  the owner or operator of the bicycle, which protects the bike from inclement weather,
  e.g., racks, lockers, or locked room, must be provided.

 4. Safety – A safe and convenient zone in which vanpool and carpool vehicles may deliver or

5. Sidewalks – Sidewalks or other designated pathways following direct and safe routes must

6. Circulation – Safe and convenient access must be maintained from the external circulation

7. Employee Parking – Employee parking must be adequately provided within the total

  from all affected public entities, including the City of Montebello and CalTrans. Before the
  City issues a building permit for any Individual Project, the Applicant must establish
  assurances, to the satisfaction of the City Engineer and/or other approving agencies, for
  the construction of the Traffic Improvements. Before the City issues a final certificate of

  Engineer and/or other approving agencies and construct all the Traffic Improvements. For

  improvements. Should the applicable entity does not approve plans to construct the off-
  site improvements within five years from the date the Applicant deposits such funds, any
  funds not being used to complete planned improvements will be returned to the
  Applicant.

M.  TRIP GENERATION
  The Director must confirm that the number of a.m., p.m., and Saturday peak hour and daily trips
  for a proposed Individual Project, based on a trip generation memorandum prepared by the
  Applicant’s transportation engineer, to determine whether or not such trips would cause the Trip
  Cap to be cumulatively exceeded. The Applicant may receive a trip credit for an existing or
  previous entitlement and/or use that was or will be discontinued.

  Trips for an Individual Project having more than one use will be calculated by adding together the
  trips generated by the portion of floor area of the Project devoted to each use unless the Director,
  based on reasonable methods, determines otherwise.

  The Applicant’s trip generation memorandum will be based on the then-current Institute of
  Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation Handbook, or such alternative rates determined
  to be appropriate by the Applicant’s transportation engineer and approved by the Director. The
  determination of trips will reflect diverted and pass-by traffic trips, the effect of interaction of
  on-site mixed-use development, the proximity of the Project to mass transit facilities, and
  implementation of other transportation demand management measures.

  If the Director disagrees with any of the trip generation factors as applied to an Individual Project,
  the Applicant may submit a proposed alternative trip generation factor for the Project, along with
  a traffic generation study prepared by transportation engineer, for review by the Planning
  Agency. Upon receiving such a study from the Applicant, the Director will cause the City Clerk to
  schedule a public hearing before the Monterey Park Planning Agency in accordance with the
  MPMC. Within 45 days after conducting a public hearing, the Planning Agency will issue written

   findings that approve, disapprove, or conditionally approve the proposed alternative Trip
  generation factor as the Trip generation factor for the Individual Project.

  VI. INDIVIDUAL PROJECT APPROVALS

A.  PROJECT CLEARANCES AND ADMINISTRATIVE DESIGN REVIEW
  1. Unless otherwise exempt, an Applicant must obtain a Project Clearance from the Director
  before the City issues any permit for an Individual Project.
  2. The Director will issue a Project Clearance if the Individual Project is in substantial
  conformance with applicable provisions of this Specific Plan and other Applicable Law and
  the applicable mitigation measures from the SEIR in Appendix A.
  3. The Applicant must pay the necessary fees consistent with the provisions of this Specific
  Plan and other Applicable Law.
  4. The Director will approve, without change or modification, an Individual Project if it is
  substantially consistent with a Conceptual Development Plan and the design
  requirements of this Specific Plan. An Applicant may submit an alternative site plan, which
  the Director will review as provided in Section A.2 above.
  5. The Director’s approval of an Individual Project also constitutes an administrative
  clearance of design review pursuant to MPMC § 21.36.060.
  6. Should the Director determine that an Individual Project is inconsistent with the
  Conceptual Development Plans or other requirements of the Specific Plan other than
  design requirements, the Director must provide detailed written findings as to any
  inconsistency to the Applicant. The Applicant may revise and resubmit the application or
  appeal the Director’s decision as provided in Chapter VIII below.
  7. If the Director determines that an Individual Project is inconsistent, or is unable to
  determine consistency, with the design requirements of the Specific Plan, the Director
  may refer the matter to the Design Review Board or Planning Commission to consider in
  accordance with the design review provisions of the MPMC. The Design Review Board
  may make recommendations to the Planning Commission, or the Planning Commission
  may, on its own authority, determine consistency with the design requirements of the
  Specific Plan. The Applicant may revise and resubmit to the Director for reconsideration
  of any design found to be inconsistent or appeal the decision as provided in Chapter VIII
  below

  The Director’s review and approval of a Project Clearance is an administrative clearance. The
  Director will act within 30 days after receiving an application for an Individual Project. If the

  A Project Clearance indicates compliance with this Specific Plan and the Applicable Law.

  A Project Clearance, including a design review consistency approval granted in accordance with
  the MPMC for an Individual Project, expires 36 months after the approval date unless within such

  authorized use commenced, or the City grants a time extension in accordance with this Section.

  expires.

  is not listed as a permitted use, the Director may determine whether the proposed use is
  similar to a permitted use and whether the use is permitted, permitted subject to
  conditions, permitted as a temporary use, or prohibited. In determining “similarity,” the

 1.  Introduction
1.1  PURPOSE OF MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM

This Mitigation Monitoring Program has been developed to provide a vehicle by which to monitor mitigation
measures and conditions of approval outlined in the 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza (MPTP) EIR, the
Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (Draft SEIR), and the Final Supplemental EIR (Final SEIR) (State
Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). The Mitigation Monitoring Program has been prepared in conformance with
Section 21081.6 of the Public Resources Code and City of Monterey Park Monitoring Requirements. Section
21081.6 states:

  (a) When making findings required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 21081 or
  when adopting a mitigated negative declaration pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision
  (c) of Section 21080, the following requirements shall apply:

  (1) The public agency shall adopt a reporting or monitoring program for the changes
  made to the project or conditions of project approval, adopted in order to mitigate or
  avoid significant effects on the environment. The reporting or monitoring program
  shall be designed to ensure compliance during project implementation. For those
  changes which have been required or incorporated into the project at the request of
  a responsible agency or a public agency having jurisdiction by law over natural
  resources affected by the project, that agency shall, if so requested by the lead or
  responsible agency, prepare and submit a proposed reporting or monitoring
  program.

  (2) The lead agency shall specify the location and custodian of the documents or other
  material which constitute the record of proceedings upon which its decision is
  based.

The Mitigation Monitoring Program will serve to document compliance with adopted/certified mitigation
measures, which are formulated to minimize impacts associated with the construction and operation of the
revised Monterey Park Market Place project (proposed project).

1.2  EIR SUMMARY

1.2.1  Previously Proposed 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza Site Plan

In March 2000, the Final EIR/EIS for the previous project was certified by the City of Monterey Park Planning
Commission. The City had the principal responsibility for project approval and acted as the CEQA lead
agency as defined by Section 15367 of the CEQA Guidelines. To help with the costs of land acquisition, site
cleanup, and required access, the City received a Section 108 Loan Guarantee and an accompanying
Economic Development Initiative grant from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
Because of the assistance provided by HUD, the project was subject to National Environmental Protection Act
(NEPA) review, and HUD was the federal (NEPA) lead agency for the previous project.

The previous site plan required the demolition of all existing buildings, excluding the LTP, and the leveling of
the berm along SR-60 on the southern portion of the site. Contaminated berm soil (with traces of lead) would
be removed from the site while the remaining soil would be used to level the site. The previously proposed

Although not included with the proposed project, a leachate treatment plant (LTP) and thermal destruction
facility (TDF) will continue to operate on the project site. Leachate is a common product of landfills, made of
groundwater and the compounds of decomposing material in the landfill. The LTP collects leachate from the
south parcel of the OII landfill and treats it. Off-gas is produced during leachate treatment and must be burned
in the treatment plant. The LTP directs off-gas to the South Parcel via a 12-inch pipeline, where it is burned
along with gas produced in the South Parcel. The TDF structure has two 60-foot high stacks, each
approximately 6 feet in diameter. It was constructed after the certification of the 2000 MPTP EIR and
improves the leachate treatment process. The structure would be contained by a chain-link fence and public
access would be restricted.

Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan

The proposed project includes the Monterey Park Market Place (MPMP) Precise Plan, which is a required
document for development within the Regional-Specialty Center (R-S) Planned Development Overlay Zone to
ensure consistency with the Monterey Park General Plan. The purpose of having a precise plan is to describe
how the proposed project would meet the requirements of the Planned Development Overlay Zone on the
project site; provide the overall design concept for the site; implement the goals, policies, and objectives of
the City’s general plan as feasible; and establish the development regulations and framework for the project
site.

Detailed building and site development standards and regulations are included in the precise plan, such as
architectural themes, building height, and types of permitted businesses. Maximum height of buildings is set
in the MPMP Precise Plan and meets the standards of the R-S Planned Development Zone Overlay, which is
50 feet or 4 stories. Architectural features are allowed to project an additional 15 feet above maximum
building height with the approval of a conditional use permit. The proposed buildings would be between 30
and 50 feet in height (up to 60 feet with architectural features).

Project Access and Parking

The existing access road for the proposed project site is Greenwood Avenue, which enters the northern
boundary of the project site from Potrero Grande Drive. The main road through the development would be
named Market Place Drive. This road would be slightly realigned where it enters the project site on the north
and then extended toward the east corner of the site. Neil Armstrong Street would no longer intersect
Paramount Avenue but would intersect Market Place Drive instead. Market Place Drive would intersect
Paramount Avenue east of the project site. With the completion of all roadway improvements, the site would
be accessible from both Potrero Grande Drive and Paramount Boulevard off of SR-60.

Market Place Drive would serve as the main public/private roadway through the retail center and it would
allow truck and standard vehicle access. Additional specified truck/service routes would allow access to the
buildings to allow for pick-up and delivery of goods. The circulation plan for the project site will identify the
primary vehicle, truck/service, and pedestrian access routes on the project site.

Onsite parking is provided based on the parking demand ratio of the proposed land uses per 1,000 square
feet of building space, as shown in the far right column in Table 1. A minimum of 2,333 spaces would be
provided, including 44 handicapped spaces throughout the site, placed near the entrances for anchor stores,
the smaller mixed retail/restaurant stores, and the retail/restaurant pads. Although 2,333 are required, up to
2,386 would be provided, which would result in a surplus of up to 53 parking spaces. All parking lots are
aboveground surface lots and would be accessible from Market Place Drive.

Alternate Land Use Scenario: Small-Box Development

An alternative layout to the revised project is also provided for the project site in the event that the project
applicant opts to develop a small-box retail shopping center instead of the big-box retail. The small-box
alternative would have a reduced total square footage of 500,000 square feet that would include 3 anchors,
up to 10 smaller retail stores, and 7 retail pads. The retail anchor stores would line the northern boundary of
the project site and retail anchor “E” (110,000 square feet) would have a garden center (30,000 square feet).
The largest anchor, Retail A (140,000 square feet), would be north of the northern Greenwood Avenue
(Market Place Drive) entrance. South of Retail A, across Market Place Drive, are Retail stores G through M.
Retail F, which is adjacent to the LTP/TDF, Retail Pad 6, and Retail Pad 7 are all more centrally located on
the site and Retail B and C and Retail Pads 1 through 5 share the northern boundary of the site with the
anchor stores. Anchor stores would have a total square footage of 321,000, and retail nonanchor stores
would have a total square footage between 139,000 and 150,000, depending on whether Retail F is

1.3  PROJECT LOCATION

The proposed Monterey Park Market Place is in the southern portion of the City of Monterey Park and borders
the City of Montebello. It would be at 2550 Greenwood Avenue, north of SR-60 between the Paramount
Boulevard and Potrero Grande Drive freeway exits. The project site is bounded by Southern California Edison
(SCE) easements on the northwest and northeast. Beyond the SCE easements are Potrero Grande Drive to
the northwest and the Resurrection Cemetery and residential land uses to the northeast and east. Greenwood
Avenue accesses the site from the north from Potrero Grande Drive; Neil Armstrong Street intersects
Paramount Boulevard to the east of the site.

1.4.3  Unavoidable Significant Adverse Impacts

With mitigation measures, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, and transportation and traffic would have
significant and unavoidable impacts

Air Quality

Impact 5.2-2

Construction emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for NOx and would cumulatively
contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. Grading emissions would be roughly the same
between the 2000 MPTP EIR and the revised MPMP Precise Plan. However, the 2000 MPTP EIR did not
identify significant construction emissions because construction activities were compared to screening
thresholds and were not modeled. SCAQMD now requires comparison to daily emissions thresholds and new
air pollutant models (e.g., URBEMIS) have been released to evaluate construction emissions. Modeling
results now show that even with implementation of Mitigation Measures 2-1 and 2-7, impacts from regional air
pollutant emissions from construction-related activities would exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance
thresholds for NOX as a result of use of heavy construction equipment. Mitigation Measure 2-7 would reduce
potentially significant impacts during Phase 1 construction activities to under the significance thresholds;
however, construction activities during Phase 2 site preparation would continue to exceed SCAQMD’s
regional significance thresholds for NOX. Therefore, impacts are significant and unavoidable. Regional
construction emissions impacts are a new significant unavoidable impact not identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR.

Impact 5.2-3

Operational phase emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for VOC, NOX, CO, PM10,
and PM2.5 and would cumulatively contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. The MPMP Precise
Plan would exceed the thresholds for VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5. Mitigation Measures 2-8 through 2-17
would reduce operational emissions, to the extent feasible. Criteria air pollutant emissions that exceed
SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds would cumulatively contribute to the NO 2, O3, and particulate
matter nonattainment designations of the SoCAB. While air quality impacts were identified in the 2000 MPTP
EIR, the MPMP Precise Plan would result in an approximately 5 to 8 percent increase in air quality impacts for
most criteria pollutants on weekdays and an approximately 44 percent increase in air quality impacts for most
criteria pollutants on weekends, compared to the 2000 MPTP. However, the project would result in a
decrease in air quality impacts based on emissions as identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR for CO (weekday
only), VOC, and NOx because of updated emission rates used in this SEIR that reflect lower emission rates
for vehicles. Further, based on the updated emission factors in the UREMIS2007 model, the revised SEIR
analysis has identified additional significant impacts associated with PM10 and PM2.5 that were not identified in
the EIR. The increase in air pollutant emissions would exceed the SCAQMD regional thresholds and therefore
the magnitude of change is considered to be significant. Modeling based on updated air pollutant emission
factors in the URBEMIS2007 model show that VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5 would exceed the significance
thresholds for the MPMP Precise Plan. Since emissions of particulate matter (PM 10 and PM2.5) were not

Greenhouse Gas Emissions

Impact 5.3-1

Project-related GHG emissions are cumulatively considerable. The MPMP Precise Plan would generate
36,509 metric tons of GHG emissions. While all feasible mitigation measures have been incorporated into the
project, the total increase in GHG emissions onsite from the project would still be substantial. The 2000 MPTP
EIR did not identify significant impacts related to GHG emissions because GHG emissions were not
incorporated into the CEQA Guidelines until March 18, 2010. GHG emissions are higher for the MPMP
Precise Plan as a result of a 17 percent increase in building square footage (600,000 square feet compared to
515,382 square feet) and 6 percent increase in average daily vehicle trips (19,719 compared to 18,674).
Since GHG emissions were not identified before, this is considered a new significant impact.

Transportation and Traffic

Impact 5.5-1

Opening Year 2015

Inasmuch as the primary responsibility for approving and/or completing certain improvements located outside
the City of Monterey Park lies with agencies other than the City of Monterey Park (i.e., City of Montebello and
Caltrans), there is the potential that significant impacts may not be fully mitigated if such improvements are
not completed for reasons beyond the City of Monterey Park’s control (e.g., the City of Monterey Park cannot
undertake or require improvements outside of Monterey Park’s jurisdiction or the City cannot construct

 2.  Mitigation Monitoring Process
2.1  MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM ORGANIZATION

CEQA requires that a reporting or monitoring program be adopted for the conditions of project approval that
are necessary to mitigate or avoid significant effects on the environment (Public Resources Code 21081.6).
The mitigation monitoring and reporting program is designed to ensure compliance with adopted mitigation
measures during project implementation. For each mitigation measure recommended in the Environmental
Impact Report, specifications are made herein that identify the action required and the monitoring that must
occur. In addition, a responsible agency is identified for verifying compliance with individual conditions of
approval contained in the Mitigation Monitoring Program (MMP). In order to effectively track and document
the status of mitigation measures, a mitigation matrix has been prepared and includes:

    Responsibility for implementation
    Timing
    Responsibility for monitoring
    Monitor

Mitigation measure timing of verification has been apportioned into several specific timing increments. Of
these, the most common are:

    Prior to project approval
    Prior to issuance of grading permit(s)
    During construction

Information pertaining to compliance with mitigation measures or any necessary modifications or refinements
will be documented in the comments portion of the matrix.

Supplement to the Certified 2000 EIR Mitigation Monitoring Program

Since this is a supplemental EIR, the MMP for this project modifies the previously adopted MMP for the
Monterey Park Towne Plaza (March 2000). The MMP for the SEIR includes the revised and new mitigation
measures for the proposed project. Where appropriate, the timing and responsible agency information from
the 2000 MMP has been retained.

2.2  MITIGATION MONITORING PROCEDURES

The City of Monterey Park Development Services Department is the designated lead agency for the Mitigation
Monitoring and Reporting Program. The City of Monterey Park includes the Mitigation Measures within the
Special Conditions of Approval. The City is responsible for review of all monitoring reports, enforcement
actions, and document disposition. The Community Development Department shall designate a Project
Mitigation Monitor for the proposed project.

 2. Mitigation Monitoring Process

2.2.1  In-Field Monitoring

The Responsible Monitoring Party shall exercise caution and professional practices at all times when
monitoring construction. Protective wear (hard hats, glasses, etc.) shall be worn at all times in construction
areas. Injuries shall be reported immediately to the Project Mitigation Monitor.

2.2.2  Coordination with Contractors

The construction manager/superintendent is responsible for coordination of contractors and for contractor
completion of required measures in accordance with the provisions of this program.

2.2.3  Recognized Experts

The use of recognized experts as a component of the monitoring team is required to ensure compliance with
scientific and engineering mitigation measures. While the recognized experts assess compliance with
required mitigation measures, consultation with the City of Monterey Park planning staff shall take place in the
event of a dispute.

2.2.4  Enforcement

Agencies may enforce conditions of approval through their existing police power, using stop-work orders,
fines, infraction citations, loss of entitlements, refusal to issue building permits or certificates of use and
occupancy or, in some cases, notice of violation for tax purposes. Criminal misdemeanor sanctions could be
available where the agency has adopted an ordinance requiring compliance with the monitoring program,
similar to the provision in many zoning ordinances that affirm the enforcement power to bring suit against
violators of the ordinances.

3.1  CATEGORIZED MITIGATION MEASURES/MATRIX

Project-specific mitigation measures and project design features (PDFs) have been categorized in matrix
format, as shown in Table 3-1. The matrix identifies the environmental factor, specific mitigation measures,
schedule, and responsible monitor. The mitigation matrix will serve as the basis for scheduling the
implementation of, and compliance with, all mitigation measures.

A supplemental EIR only discusses new environmental impacts that would result from a change in the project
description between the original and revised projects and it only needs to contain the information necessary to
make the previous EIR adequate for the project as revised (CEQA Guidelines Section 15163). To avoid
certain environmental impacts, the City of Monterey Park has included certain PDFs, which are considered
part of the proposed project. The PDFs are mandatory and will be adopted by the City of Monterey Park as
part of the project’s conditions of approval. Both the PDFs and mitigation measures are part of the MMP to
be implemented by the City of Monterey Park. To provide a complete matrix that may be used for monitoring
and enforcement, this mitigation monitoring program includes mitigation measures and project design
features associated with the new impacts caused by the proposed project, as well as all mitigation measures
which remain effective from the previously certified 2000 MPTP EIR.

3.2  LONG-TERM MONITORING

Long-term monitoring related to several mitigation measures will be required, including fire safety inspections.
Postconstruction fire inspections are conducted on a routine basis by the City of Monterey Park Fire
Department.

 4.  Mitigation Monitoring Reports
Mitigation monitoring reports are required to document compliance with the Mitigation Monitoring Program
and to dispute arbitration enforcement resolution. Specific reports include:

    Field Check Report
    Implementation Compliance Report
    Arbitration/Enforcement Report

4.1  FIELD CHECK REPORT

Field check reports are required to record in-field compliance and conditions.

4.2  IMPLEMENTATION COMPLIANCE REPORT

The Implementation Compliance Report (ICR) is prepared to document the implementation of mitigation
measures on a phased basis, based on the information in Table 3-1. The report summarizes implementation
compliance, including mitigation measures, date completed, and monitor’s signature.

4.3  ARBITRATION/ENFORCEMENT REPORT

The Arbitration/Enforcement Report (AER) is prepared to document the outcome of arbitration committee
review and becomes a portion of the ICR.

  Agreement (the “Amended and Restated Development Agreement”) in
  connection with possible revisions to the Approved Project to allow the
  development of its final phase with retail, auto dealership, last mile distribution,
  and/or warehouse uses, parking, and related improvements, as further
  described in the specific plan (“Specific Plan”) being considered in conjunction
  with the Amended and Restated Development Agreement (the “Project”). The
  Amended and Restated Development Agreement is attached to this Ordinance

  time, place and purpose of the public hearing was duly provided in accordance

  Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 21.32.070.

  April 5, 2023

On September 16, 2021, Monterey Park Retail Partners Tract 3, LLC, submitted a request
for a conditional use permit (“CUP”) to add a fourth drive through restaurant at the Market
Place development that the City Council approved December 19, 2012 (the “Project”).
The Market Place Precise Plan allowed up to three drive-through restaurants be approved
ministerially; any subsequent drive-throughs require a CUP. The general layout, uses,
parking, and traffic patterns are all the same as originally contemplated by the City Council
on December 19, 2012.

The Project is considered a “project” under the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”). Accordingly, environmental review is required pursuant to CEQA (Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code of
Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.).

Background

On December 19, 2012, the Monterey Park City Council adopted Resolution No. 11548
certifying the Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (SEIR) for the Market
Place project and adopting a Statement of Overriding Considerations (see Final EIR/EIS
at State Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). Implementation of mitigation measures
identified in the SEIR will be monitored as called for in the Mitigation Monitoring and
Reporting Program adopted on December 19, 2012.

The circumstances, impacts, and mitigation requirements identified in the SEIR remain
applicable to the proposed Project; there are no new issues and the level of environmental
impacts identified in the SEIR is static.

Environmental Analysis

CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2) states that if a project is proposed which has been the
subject of a prior certified EIR, and “[i]f the [City] finds that pursuant to Section 15162, no
new effects could occur or new mitigation measures would be required, the agency can
approve the activity as being within the scope of the project covered by the … EIR, and
no new environmental document would be required.”
CEQA Guidelines § 15162 defines the conditions under which a subsequent EIR would
be required for a project as follows:
 (1)  Substantial changes are proposed in the project which require major revisions of
  the EIR due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or
  substantial increase in the severity of previously identified significant effects;

retail uses has become less easily achieved. The additional uses of a last-mile distribution

proposed Specific Plan sets up the framework to allow the above listed uses.

With the additional alternative uses proposed in the Market Place Specific Plan, the
applicant has included a Level of Service and Vehicle Miles Traveled Screening Analysis
to support an auto dealership which will result in fewer trips generated than the build-out
of Phase 3 with retail uses analyzed as part of the FEIR and SEIR for the overall project.
In a case where, a last mile distribution center or warehouse use is proposed, a similar
traffic analysis will be necessary to ensure that those developments are not exceeding
the traffic that was contemplated in the SEIR.

The proposed Specific Plan is consistent with the applicable General Plan Elements of
the Land Use, Circulation, Safety and Community Service, Resource, and housing Goals
and Policies as analyzed in the General Plan. Overall, the Specific Plan contains unique
development standards and design guidelines to ensure that commercial development
will be compatible with the site and existing development around the Specific Plan Area.

architectural design for the future development at the Market Place.

Development Agreement

Chapter 21.44 of the MPMC requires Development Agreements (DA) for large scale
projects that require multiple entitlements and long-term commitment of both public and
private resources. The original approval of the Market Place included a DA that was
approved in 2013. However, with the new scenarios presented in Phase 3 of the project,
a new DA (DA-22-01) is proposed to allow for the uses proposed and an updated public
benefit payment. While the MPMC generally imposes a term of five years for development
agreements – which is intended to facilitate the prompt development of approved projects
– the City Council may change the term in its discretion. Here, the draft DA proposes an
initial term of five years with two automatic renewals of two years each; these renewals
would occur unless the DA were terminated not later than 90 days before the anniversary
date (Section 20 of the DA). As a result, the applicant would have an extended time within
which to construct improvements and the City would receive additional public benefit
payments as contemplated by Section 6(c) of the DA. Assuming that the DA were in effect
for the full nine-year term and the development was fully built out, the City could receive
up to approximately $1.6M in public benefit payments.

during the term of the DA which could amount to a total amount of approximately $1.6M.

Place is shared with the City of Montebello via a Sharing Sales Tax Agreement. Sales
tax revenue payments are payable by Monterey Park to Montebello at a rate of 18%
from the generated sales tax. There is no sunset to the sharing agreement.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
This Ordinance was reviewed pursuant to CEQA. Adopting this Ordinance is exempt from
further environmental review because it establishes rules and procedures for operation
of existing facilities; minor temporary use of land; minor alterations in land use; new
construction of small structures; and minor structures accessory to existing commercial
facilities. The Ordinance, therefore, is categorically exempt from further environmental
review under CEQA Guidelines §§ 15301; 15303, 15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further,
adopting the ordinance is exempt from environmental review pursuant to CEQA
Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because the ordinance is for general policies and procedure-
making. It can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the Ordinance may
have a significant effect on the environment. Individual projects utilizing these regulations
will each be separately subject to an environmental assessment. Finally, this Ordinance
is exempt from further environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15269(a)
because the protection of public and private property is necessary to maintain service
essential to the public, health and welfare.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
MPMC Chapter 13.12 regulates encroachments and construction within all public right of
ways within the City. The regulations under this chapter were first implemented in the
1980s and are stale in comparison to industry standards. The proposed ordinance
updates regulations for excavations and encroachments on, over, and under public rights-
of-ways and public service easements.

BACKGROUND:
Government Code Section 38775 permits the City to regulate and prohibit encroachments
into and obstructions on public property. An encroachment includes, without limitation,
the following:
   Any construction work performed within public rights-of-ways or public service
  easements;
   Any work other than construction work performed within a public right-of-way or
  public service easement that obstructs, or interferes with the use of, the public
  right-of-way or public service easement; and
   Any structure or object that is placed or installed within a public right-of-way or
  within a public service easement in a manner that obstructs or otherwise interferes
  with the use of the public right-of-way or public service easement.

The proposed ordinance repeals and replaces current provisions and procedures under
MPMC Chapter 13.12 and provides new permit requirements, including, exceptions to
permits, procedures for permit application process, permit insurance requirements,
guidelines for excavation in recently resurfaced public streets, requirements for traffic
control plans and procedures for administrative review of permit decisions. The Ordinance
also includes an encroachment permit application form and general conditions of approval
applicable to all encroachments in the City.

SECTION 1: Findings. The City Council finds and declares that:

  A.  Government Code § 38775 permits the City to regulate and prohibit
  encroachments into and obstructions on public property and may provide
  for the removal of any prohibited encroachments;

  B.  Government Code § 38771 permits general law cities to identify public
  nuisances by ordinance;

  C.  The regulations in Chapter 13.12 of the Monterey Park Municipal Code
  (“MPMC”) are substantially unchanged from the 1980s and do not reflect
  modern policies and procedures;

  D.  It is in the public interest for the City to take appropriate actions to protect
  citizens and their property from conditions that threaten public health,
  safety, and welfare by adopting modern policies and procedures concerning
  encroachments into the public right-of-ways; and

  E.  The City reviewed this Ordinance pursuant to the California Environmental
  Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regulations §§15000,
  et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA and the CEQA Guidelines are
  collectively referred to as “CEQA Regulations.”

“Encroachments and Obstructions” is amended in its entirety to read as follows:

13.12.020. Definitions.

  Unless the contrary is stated or clearly appears from the context, the
  following definitions will govern the construction of the words and phrases
  used in this chapter:

  A.  “Administrator” means the public works director, or designee.

  B.  “Encroachment” means any construction work performed within public
  rights-of-ways or public service easements; any work other than
  construction work performed within a public right-of-way or public service
  easement that obstructs, or interferes with the use of, the public right-of-
  way or public service easement; and any structure or object that is placed
  or installed within a public right-of-way or within a public service easement
  in a manner that obstructs or otherwise interferes with the use of the
  public right-of-way or public service easement.

  C.  “Excavation” means removal of any concrete, asphalt, road, earth, or
  other, similar, surface materials covering a public right-of-way or public
  service easement.

  D.  “Public Right-of-Way” means any city street, sidewalk, pedestrian path,
  bike path or any other “public way,” as defined by Streets and Highways
  Code § 18609.

  E.  “Public Service Easement” means any public sewer easement, public
  storm drain easement, public utility easement or other “public service
  easement,” as defined in Streets and Highways Code § 8306.

13.12.030. Permit Required.

  A.  Permit Required. Unless otherwise provided by applicable law, it is
  unlawful for any person to make any encroachment or excavation in any
  public right-of-way or service easement, without first obtaining a permit
  issued pursuant to this chapter.

  B.  A permit is not valid until the administrator receives the applicant’s written
  acceptance in accordance with this chapter.

  C.  During City business hours, persons must immediately notify the
  Administrator of emergency encroachment work for all repairs performed
  on existing infrastructure. Should emergency repair work commence
  during other than normal City business hours, the person must notify the
  Administrator of work performed by 9:00 am on the following business
  day. An encroachment permit application must be submitted to the
  Administrator within three business days.

13.12.040. Planting Vegetation.

  It is unlawful for any person to place or plant, or cause to be placed or
  planted, any tree, shrub or bush in any public right-of-way or public service
  easement without obtaining a permit pursuant to this chapter. In addition to
  all other conditions of this chapter, a permit planting trees will specify the
  place for planting, the distance apart, the kind of trees and such other
  matters specified by the administrator.

13.12.050. Street Damage by Moving Vehicles.

  Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, it is unlawful for any person to
  drive, drag, propel or move, or cause to be moved upon any public right-of-
  way or public service easement, any plow, harrow or cutting or scratching
  instrument or any heavy vehicle or machine liable to break the surface of,
  or do injury to the public right-of-way or public service easement.

13.12.060. Excavation in Recently Resurfaced Public Streets.

  A.  Except as otherwise allowed by this chapter, public streets that were
  resurfaced with an emulsified asphalt “slurry” or asphalt “cape seal” within
  the previous two years or improved with asphalt/concrete within the
  previous five years of the proposed excavation may not be excavated for
  utilities or for other reasons.

  B.  A permit may be issued to allow a permittee to encroach within a public
  street to install utility facilities, or for other purposes, if such work can be
  accomplished by boring under the public street section or by other
  trenchless technologies. Alternative methods for such work including,
  without limitation, relocating utility facilities to areas other than the public
  street (for example, under public sidewalks and/or parkways) will be
  considered and determined not to be feasible before a permit may be
  issued pursuant to this chapter. Any additional costs for, without limitation,
  relocating utility facilities outside of the public street or boring under the
  public street must be borne by the permittee.

  C.  Excavation of a public street may be allowed by permit under only the
  most unusual circumstances if the Administrator determines that
  relocation or boring is not feasible. Under such circumstances, the
  Administrator will require a permittee to meet the city’s construction
  standards for excavating in recently resurfaced streets, pay all costs
  associated with such excavation, and provide such additional security to
  ensure the integrity of the recently resurfaced public street as may be
  reasonable required by the Administrator.

13.12.070. Exceptions to Permit Requirements.

  A permit is not required for the following encroachments or excavations:

  A.  United States mailboxes;

  B.  Poles and facilities of public utilities lawfully using the public streets of the
  city;

  C.  Portable and usual garbage and rubbish receptacles when conforming to
  and placed in accordance with the rules and regulations of the City;

  D.  Work required by a valid public works contract between the city and a
  contractor;

  E.  An encroachment made pursuant to a subdivision improvement
  agreement between the city and a developer;

  F.  Encroachments or excavations related to filming activities where the
  person possesses a filming permit issued pursuant to this code;

  G.  Encroachments or excavations authorized by a permit issued pursuant to
  this code for parades, athletic events, or public assemblies;

  H.  An encroachment made by adjoining property owner for installing concrete
  flat work in a parkway between a public street and sidewalk or for the
  purpose of installing concrete flat work behind a public sidewalk, provided
  the concrete flat work does not consist of more than 25-percent hardscape
  within each parkway area, and has otherwise been approved by the city;

  I.  An encroachment made by a city officer or employee acting within the
  course or scope of such officer’s or employee’s duties or employment; and

  J.  An encroachment made by the owner or lessee of property adjoining a
  public right-of-way within the central commercial zoning district for a
  sidewalk café pursuant to a license or permit issued pursuant to this code
  authorizing the use of the right-of-way for such a purpose.

13.12.080. Administration.

  The administrator will administer this chapter, including, without limitation,

  undertaking any of the enforcement actions allowed by this chapter.

SECTION 3: Environmental Assessment. This Ordinance was reviewed pursuant to
CEQA. Adopting this Ordinance is exempt from further environmental review because it
establishes rules and procedures for operation of existing facilities; minor temporary use
of land; minor alterations in land use; new construction of small structures; and minor
structures accessory to existing commercial facilities. The Ordinance, therefore, is
categorically exempt from further CEQA review under CEQA Guidelines §§ 15301;
15303, 15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further, the adopting the ordinance is also exempt
from review under CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because the
ordinance is for general policies and procedure-making. It can be seen with certainty that
there is no possibility that the Ordinance may have a significant effect on the environment.
Individual projects utilizing these regulations will each be separately subject to an
environmental assessment. Finally, this Ordinance is exempt from further review pursuant
to CEQA Guidelines § 15269(a) because the protection of public and private property is
necessary to maintain service essential to the public, health and welfare.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  This Ordinance was reviewed pursuant to CEQA. Adopting this Ordinance is exempt from further
  environmental review because it establishes rules and procedures for operation of existing
  facilities; minor temporary use of land; minor alterations in land use; new construction of small
  structures; and minor structures accessory to existing commercial facilities. The Ordinance,
  therefore, is categorically exempt from further environmental review under CEQA Guidelines §§
  15301; 15303, 15304(e); 15305; and 15311. Further, adopting the ordinance is exempt from
  environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because the ordinance is for
  general policies and procedure-making. It can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility
